title: Mountains walking
hookLine: Dogen's teaching that the blue mountains are always walking

lines: THE BLUE MOUNTAINS ARE ALWAYS WALKING.
THEN HE TURNS IT ON YOU.
cards: A mountain is the stock picture of something that doesn't move. People say steady as a mountain.

So it's startling to open another of Dogen's essays, the Mountains and Waters Sutra, and find him passing on an old Chan teacher's saying, in paraphrase: the blue mountains are always walking. Not once, long ago. Always.
And then he turns it on the reader.

teach.h: AN OLD CHAN LINE, A DOGEN ESSAY.
teach.b: First, where it comes from. Dogen quotes the line from an earlier Chan teacher, Furong Daokai, and builds an essay around it. The essay is part of his larger collection, the Shobogenzo.
Second, what he says about it. In paraphrase: the mountains' walking is just like people's walking; don't doubt it because it doesn't look like human walking.

teach.h: DOUBT THE MOUNTAINS, DOUBT YOUR WALK.
teach.b: Then the turn: if you doubt the mountains walking, you don't yet understand your own walking. The puzzle isn't really about rocks. It's about how you see anything at all.

teach.h: TIME, OR A HABIT OF SEEING?
teach.b: Third, time, or a habit of seeing? Readers hear it more than one way. Some hear it about time: the mountain you're looking at is never quite the same mountain twice.

Wind, water, seasons and light move through it, and it moves through them. Some hear it about seeing: the idea that a mountain sits still while you're the one going places is a habit of the mind, not the whole truth.
Dogen doesn't settle it with a single explanation. He keeps the line strange on purpose.

teach.h: WHAT LOOKS FIXED IS STILL MOVING.
teach.b: Fourth, what looks fixed is still moving. It's easy to treat certain things as fixed: a parent, a hometown, a job, one's own personality.
That's just how it is. This teaching gently loosens that. What looks fixed may be quietly moving.
And the self that thinks it's the only thing on the road may be standing still more than it knows.

how: Zen students read Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra (Sansuikyo) from the Shobogenzo, often in study groups, and teachers return to its line about the walking mountains to unsettle fixed ways of seeing.

games.q: you read the line: the blue mountains are always walking. your first thought is, mountains don't walk. what does Dogen say to that?
o: you're right, it's only a metaphor.
if you doubt their walking, you don't yet understand your own.
games.why: Dogen turns the doubt back on the reader: the puzzle is about how you see, including how you see your own walking.

practice: Rest your eyes on a hill, a tree, a building or even a wall, or picture a mountain you've seen, and let it be still.

Then slowly notice what is moving in it or through it: light changing, air, shadows, the life on it, the way your own looking shifts. Don't decide what it means; just wonder, as Dogen invites: is it walking?
